feed.title: Wits AHEAD · Daily briefing
feed.subtitle: News, research, video and readings on AI, data and human capability in higher education, curated every morning.
feed.rights: Wits AHEAD Research Group, Wits School of Education, University of the Witwatersrand

entry.title: University of Colorado system adopts a living policy for responsible use of AI
entry.summary:
The University of Colorado system's new Administrative Policy Statement 6012, Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence, took effect on 24 August 2026 and was set out on the university's policy blog on 21 September. It establishes systemwide expectations for academic integrity, data protection, transparency and verifying AI-generated content for accuracy, and is explicitly presented as a policy meant to evolve as feedback comes in from students and staff.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, a large public university system choosing to treat its AI rules as a living document rather than a fixed policy is a Global North comparator for the governance choices Wits AHEAD tracks in the Global South.

University of Colorado · University policy announcement

entry.title: University of Pretoria trains future teachers in "prompt literacy" for the AI classroom
entry.summary:
Researchers in the University of Pretoria's Department of Early Childhood Education, led by Dr Joyce West and Dr Kayla Willemse, are running a multi-phase study on prompt literacy, the ability to give generative AI clear instructions while critically judging what it produces. The project trains future teachers to use AI as a collaborative classroom tool rather than a threat, through activities such as building children's stories and digital materials, while keeping a close eye on bias, inaccuracy and copyright in what the AI generates.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 3, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, the study addresses a gap Wits AHEAD watches closely: whether new teachers are actually taught how to question AI output, not only how to produce it.

Future SA, reporting University of Pretoria research · South African higher education press, reporting university research

entry.title: East African universities and Arizona State University partner to build "AI-ready" higher education
entry.summary:
The Inter-University Council for East Africa, the East African Community's higher education body, announced a partnership on 9 September 2026 with Arizona State University's University Design Institute to help East African universities become AI-ready. The work covers four areas: leadership and governance, faculty development, research ecosystems and cross-institutional learning. The Design Institute brings experience from 26 countries and more than 140 institutions, including seven in Africa.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 5, analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, the partnership shows a regional higher education body building AI capacity across many universities at once, a model Wits AHEAD can compare against its own reach in Southern Africa.

Inter-University Council for East Africa · Intergovernmental higher education body announcement

entry.title: Maharashtra sets up a state committee to govern AI and data dashboards across its universities
entry.summary:
Maharashtra's Higher and Technical Education Department has issued a government resolution setting up an AI, Data Analytics and Dashboard Governance Committee, chaired by Professor Rajnish Kamat, vice-chancellor of Shivaji University, Kolhapur. Over its three-year term the nine-member committee must set a state AI strategy, choose priority uses for generative AI, machine learning and natural language processing, standardise data across the state's existing student, examination and scholarship dashboards, and build automated trend analysis and risk forecasting into a portal that currently only reports numbers, while meeting cybersecurity and privacy rules. It reports every quarter to the department's most senior civil servants.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 5, analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, this is one of the first state governments anywhere to put a standing, accountable committee in charge of turning a reporting dashboard into a genuine early-warning and decision-support system, a model Wits AHEAD can point to when arguing for the same shift in South Africa.

Government of Maharashtra, Higher and Technical Education Department · State government resolution, reported by regional press

entry.title: Telkom Foundation, BCX and Alibaba Cloud partner with Wits to give students AI-powered coding tools
entry.summary:
Telkom Foundation, BCX and Alibaba Cloud have partnered with the University of the Witwatersrand to give about 165 third-year Computer Science students access to Alibaba's Qoder AI-powered development platform for their academic software projects. The Qoder Programme is meant to give students hands-on experience of AI-assisted coding tools before they enter a workplace where such tools are now standard, and to strengthen the link between the Wits curriculum and industry practice. Professor Richard Klein, head of the Wits School of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics, said the curriculum needs to evolve alongside these global developments.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, this is a concrete step by Wits itself to close the gap between what computer science graduates learn and the AI-augmented software engineering roles they will enter, at a scale Wits AHEAD can track and build on.

Wits University · University announcement

entry.title: Systematic review of 124 studies finds AI's value in education depends on governance, not the technology, and flags a Global South research gap

category.term: Global (evidence base: Central Asia, East Africa)

entry.summary:
A systematic narrative review by researchers based at universities in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tanzania synthesised 124 studies published between January 2020 and January 2026 on how artificial intelligence is reshaping education. It found a real but uneven shift from isolated AI tools towards more adaptive, data-informed teaching, and concluded that whether this shift helps or harms learners depends on governance and institutional context rather than the technology itself, and that human judgement and the teacher's role must stay central rather than treating AI as an autonomous authority. The authors also found the evidence base itself skewed heavily towards English-language scholarship, with Global South, indigenous and multilingual perspectives still largely missing.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, this is a peer-reviewed confirmation, from researchers themselves based in Central Asia and East Africa, of the exact evidence gap that motivates Wits AHEAD's own work: the literature meant to guide AI policy in education barely includes the Global South voices it should be guided by.

Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Business schools bring back oral defences as AI use rises
entry.summary:
Leading European business schools, among them Insead, Imperial College Business School and HEC Paris, are reintroducing oral defences, pen-and-paper exams and closely supervised assessment because generative AI has undermined the standard take-home case study. Imperial's Peter Todd said staff can no longer be confident what a written submission represents unless students defend it in person or write it under supervision, and HEC Paris now alternates between assessments done with computers and without them. The Graduate Management Admission Council said assessment standards need to be clearer if business qualifications are to keep their meaning.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, this shows leading business schools abandoning take-home assessment altogether rather than patching it, which matters directly for how Wits AHEAD frames assessment integrity guidance for African universities facing the same pressure with far fewer resources for oral or supervised exams.

Times Higher Education · Established higher education press

entry.title: African curriculum experts meet in Dar es Salaam to confront the AI challenge in teacher education
entry.summary:
The Sixth Conference of the African Curriculum Association was held in Dar es Salaam from 22 to 25 September 2026, bringing together curriculum developers, teacher trainers, researchers and policymakers from across the continent. Tanzania Institute of Education director general Dr Aneth Komba and ACA secretary general Dr Gertrude Namubiru led discussions on how African curricula and teacher preparation must adapt to artificial intelligence and rapid technological change while staying grounded in local skills and community needs. The conference set out to produce a Dar es Salaam Declaration on Education Transformation in Africa, aligned with the African Union's Agenda 2063 and the fourth Sustainable Development Goal.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 3, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, a continent-wide gathering setting out how teacher preparation itself must change for an AI-shaped classroom speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's work on what teacher educators need to know, not only what pupils and students should be taught.

The Citizen (Tanzania) · Established national press

entry.title: Universities must teach people to work ‘with AI, not for AI’, says King's College London head
entry.summary:
Speaking at the 2026 Korea Times Global Conference in Seoul, King's College London vice-chancellor Shitij Kapur said universities must ensure people work with artificial intelligence rather than for it. He set out five responsibilities for universities: redefining what learning means, preparing graduates for a changing labour market, protecting thoughtful scholarship, advancing AI for the collective good and making sure the technology strengthens rather than replaces human capability. Kapur argued that AI's development is not fixed, and that universities and nations can still shape how it is built and used rather than simply accepting it from the technology industry.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, a leading vice-chancellor putting universities at the centre of shaping AI rather than merely reacting to it supports Wits AHEAD's own case that higher education in the Global South should help set the terms of AI adoption, not just absorb tools built elsewhere.

University World News · Established higher education press

entry.title: Latin America's universities embrace AI faster than they can govern it, new study finds
entry.summary:
A UNESCO IESALC study of 200 higher education institutions across 19 Latin American and Caribbean countries found that 87 per cent already use artificial intelligence in some part of their work, yet only 26 per cent have any formal AI framework. Adoption is highest among private non-profit universities, at 84 per cent, against 68 per cent for public institutions and 52 per cent for private for-profit providers, and 55 per cent of universities overall have no dedicated AI budget. UNESCO's Borhene Chakroun said maximising the benefits depends on sustained investment in access and capacity, with governance that ensures ethical use, transparency and accountability.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, this shows the gap Wits AHEAD warns against taking hold at scale: public universities, which serve the students with fewest alternatives, are adopting AI fastest in the classroom while lagging furthest behind on governance, training and funding to use it responsibly.

Times Higher Education · Established higher education press, reporting a UNESCO IESALC study

entry.title: African universities can drive talent development at scale, Mastercard Foundation tells Accra convening
entry.summary:
At the inaugural Higher Education Transformation Convening in Accra on 22 September 2026, the Mastercard Foundation's Dr John Nkengasong described African universities as 'engines of prosperity' and human capital infrastructure that must align teaching with labour markets and industry. The event recognised five institutions with the Africa Higher Education for Transformation (AHEFT) Prize: Addis Ababa University, 2iE, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Muni University and the University of Rwanda. The foundation restated its goal of helping 30 million young Africans, 70 per cent of them women, into dignified work by 2030.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, a major funder framing universities as talent infrastructure, while naming AI as a force reshaping work, strengthens the case for Wits AHEAD's evidence on which graduate capabilities actually lead to dignified work in African labour markets.

University World News · Established higher education press

entry.title: 'Syncopathy' and AI: African HE must choose verification
entry.summary:
Writing in University World News, Dr Kende Kefale of the University of Cape Town coins 'syncopathy' for AI outputs, such as citations and arguments, that look plausible but skip verification, and argues that universities share the same flaw because checking work is costly and invisible while output is cheap and easy to count. He proposes that institutions disclose how much work receives human examination before credentials are conferred, that every automated detection system have a named person accountable for its errors, and that verification records become a lasting institutional output. He points to South Africa's draft National AI Policy, withdrawn in April 2026 after fabricated citations were found in its reference list.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the argument gives Wits AHEAD a practical frame for AI governance in African universities, one that places the cost of verification and accountability for automated judgements with institutions rather than with students.

University World News · Commentary by a University of Cape Town academic in established higher education press

entry.title: From AI use to funding cuts: how provosts are navigating 2026
entry.summary:
Inside Higher Ed's 2026 survey of 376 chief academic officers, fielded by Hanover Research, finds that about seven in ten provosts use AI in their own work at least weekly, yet only one in ten says their institution has a centralised AI strategy. Only 12 per cent report department workflow gains from institutional AI investment and 8 per cent institution-wide transformation, while 15 per cent have not invested at all. Skills and staff capacity (51 per cent) and faculty and staff resistance (50 per cent) are the main barriers cited.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 5, analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, the gap between leaders' personal use of AI and institutional strategy is exactly the space where Wits AHEAD argues for evidence-led, system-level decisions about AI in universities.

Inside Higher Ed · Established higher education press; national survey fielded by Hanover Research

entry.title: Record number of graduates pushes youth unemployment to 18.9%
entry.summary:
Urban unemployment among 16 to 24 year olds in China, excluding students, rose to 18.9 per cent in August 2026 from 17.9 per cent in July, according to National Bureau of Statistics figures reported by University World News. The rise followed a record 12.7 million university graduates this summer and is the highest reading since the methodology changed in 2023. The report points to weak domestic demand and the growing adoption of artificial intelligence as pressures on entry-level hiring.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, China's graduate squeeze shows that expanding higher education does not on its own secure entry into work when AI is reshaping entry-level roles, a lesson Wits AHEAD will weigh against graduate labour markets in South Africa and the wider Global South.

University World News (from the South China Morning Post) · Established higher education press reporting national statistics

entry.title: Ten-country African university alliance pushes joint research and AI skills
entry.summary:
The Alliance for Africa Partnership, a consortium of 12 institutions across 10 African countries anchored by Michigan State University, used its annual meeting in Dar es Salaam on 22 September 2026 to call for closer joint research and for universities to build artificial intelligence skills into their curricula. Professor Nelson Boniface of the University of Dar es Salaam told delegates that AI competency is now a basic requirement for every graduate, not only for those who code, and urged stronger links between universities, industry and government to turn research into practical problem solving.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 4 covers AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions. A ten-country African university alliance putting AI skills and joint research on its own agenda, without waiting for outside frameworks, is a live example of the cross-border collaboration Wits AHEAD studies and a reminder that the continent's skills gap is being addressed from within.

Tanzania Daily News, via allAfrica · African press wire service

entry.title: Report warns AI adoption in US colleges is outpacing student safeguards
entry.summary:
A new report from Student Defense's SHAPE initiative, covered by Inside Higher Ed on 18 September 2026, finds that United States colleges have woven artificial intelligence into admissions, financial aid, advising and teaching faster than they have built safeguards to protect students. It identifies algorithmic bias in aid decisions, data privacy gaps and a loss of authentic learning communities as the main risks, and calls on institutions to set clear governance and transparency rules before deploying AI systems further.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the report is a concrete checklist of where AI governance in higher education is falling behind practice, useful for testing Wits AHEAD's own guidance on transparency and accountability against a system further down the adoption curve.

Inside Higher Ed · Established higher education press

entry.title: UNESCO: over 25 education ministers declare AI must serve the 'common good'
entry.summary:
More than 25 education ministers and senior officials meeting at UNESCO's Digital Learning Week in Paris adopted a joint statement on 8 September 2026 declaring that education must remain a human right and a common good as artificial intelligence spreads through classrooms and universities. The statement sets out eight priorities, including keeping AI systems auditable and subject to public oversight, and protecting teachers' say over classroom technology. It cited a UNESCO survey in which 93 per cent of academics believed students were using generative AI to produce assignments, and 63 per cent perceived a decline in students' cognitive capacities.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, a ministerial statement of this scale gives Wits AHEAD an internationally endorsed benchmark for what public accountability in AI governance should look like, one that universities and national policymakers in the Global South can cite directly.

UNESCO · UN agency ministerial statement

entry.title: University of Alaska regents weigh a system-wide AI policy for every campus
entry.summary:
The University of Alaska's Board of Regents has reviewed a draft artificial intelligence policy that would require all three of its campuses to put in place an AI implementation plan for students, staff and faculty. The draft sets out guiding principles on preserving human judgement, protecting data privacy and security, and using AI to widen access to education services, with feedback sessions planned through autumn 2026 and final approval targeted for the November regents meeting.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 6 covers responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy. A public university system building its AI governance from first principles, in public and with regents raising questions about monitoring capacity, is a useful governance model for Wits AHEAD to track as it develops its own policy guidance.

Alaska Public Media · Public broadcaster report

entry.title: World Bank opens free AI skills training to young people across 44 African countries
entry.summary:
The World Bank has launched 'The Job I Hope For', inviting young people aged 18 and over across 44 Sub-Saharan African countries to register for free online training in generative AI fundamentals, prompt writing and AI ethics, delivered in English and French in October 2026. The programme responds to a continent where more than 600 million young people are expected to enter the labour market by 2050, asking participants to first set out the career they hope for before building the AI skills to reach it.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 4 covers AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions. A continent-wide, free AI skills programme aimed squarely at youth entering the workforce is a direct test of how training at scale can be built for the labour markets Wits AHEAD studies, and a possible partner or model to watch.

World Bank · Intergovernmental body brief

entry.title: Systematic review finds AI training for future primary maths teachers is still too brief to stick
entry.summary:
A systematic review by researchers at three Portuguese universities examined 11 peer-reviewed studies on how pre-service primary school teachers are trained to use AI in mathematics teaching. Most training ran as short sessions bolted onto existing courses rather than sustained modules, and covered AI awareness and practical use well but ethics and critical evaluation only inconsistently, leaving little evidence that skills transfer into real classrooms.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 3 covers AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education. The review's four essential dimensions, awareness, literacy and prompting, pedagogical integration and critical evaluation, give Wits AHEAD a concrete checklist for designing its own teacher-training work rather than a one-off AI workshop.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed systematic review

entry.title: New scale measures students' skill at using AI responsibly in assessed work
entry.summary:
Researchers at three institutions in China have developed and validated an eighteen-item scale that measures how well higher education students understand assessment criteria, disclose their use of AI and preserve academic integrity when using generative AI in coursework. Tested with 486 students and then a separate 798, the scale showed a reliable five-factor structure and was strongly linked to how much students engaged with feedback and their intention to act with integrity.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 1 covers generative AI in higher education: teaching, assessment and integrity. A validated instrument like this gives institutions a practical way to measure and build students' assessment literacy, rather than relying only on detection software or blanket bans.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Prescriptive AI model flags Ecuadorian students at highest dropout risk, and what would change it
entry.summary:
Researchers at a public university in Ecuador built a prescriptive analytics framework, tracking 2,500 students who entered between 2020 and 2024, that not only predicted dropout risk with high accuracy (ROC-AUC 0.95 to 0.97) but identified the smallest feasible changes, such as an extra early credit or better home internet access, that would move a student out of the highest-risk group. Foundation-year grades, early credit progress, socioeconomic vulnerability and home internet access were the strongest predictors.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 2 covers AI and predictive analytics for student success. This moves early-warning analytics from simply flagging at-risk students to prescribing specific, low-cost interventions, a model Wits AHEAD can point to for student-success work in similarly resourced settings.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Largest meta-analysis yet finds AI-supported STEM teaching has a real, moderate effect on learning
entry.summary:
A meta-analysis pooling 35 experimental and quasi-experimental studies has found that AI-supported instruction produces a statistically significant, moderate positive effect on STEM learning outcomes (g = 0.67). Gains were strongest for high school students, and interventions lasting one to two months proved the most effective duration tested.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 3 covers AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education. This is among the clearest quantitative evidence yet that AI-supported STEM teaching works, and the finding on optimal intervention length is directly useful for how Wits AHEAD designs and times its own STEM programmes.

Journal of Intelligence · Peer-reviewed meta-analysis

entry.title: Gates Foundation commits 1 billion US dollars over two years to equitable AI
entry.summary:
The Gates Foundation has pledged at least 1 billion US dollars over the next two years to build and deliver equitable artificial intelligence, with 400 million earmarked for education, 400 million for health, 100 million for agriculture and 100 million for AI training data in underserved languages. The pledge accompanies the foundation's tenth Goalkeepers report, titled Make This Matter: AI, Equity and the Choice We Can't Delay.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 6 asks who is designing AI responsibly and for whom. A philanthropic pledge of this scale, aimed at closing the gap for the poorest regions, will shape which AI-in-education tools reach the Global South classrooms Wits AHEAD studies.

Gates Foundation · Foundation press release accompanying its Goalkeepers report

entry.title: Systematic review of 105 studies finds Africa and Oceania missing from generative AI teacher research
entry.summary:
A PRISMA-guided review of 105 peer-reviewed studies on teachers and generative AI, published since 2023 in leading educational technology journals, finds the evidence base concentrated in China, Turkey, the United States and Spain, with Africa and Oceania markedly underrepresented. AI literacy, pedagogical knowledge and self-efficacy, framed through the TPACK model, are the strongest predictors of effective classroom integration, ahead of simple access to tools.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 3 covers AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education. A review this size confirms that Wits AHEAD's own research on African teacher education fills a documented gap rather than duplicating a saturated field.

Education Sciences (MDPI) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Stanford study finds a persistent 19% AI employment gap for young workers
entry.summary:
Stanford's Digital Economy Lab reports that employment among 22 to 25 year olds in occupations most exposed to artificial intelligence is now 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less exposed peers, up from 15% a year earlier. The gap operates mainly through reduced hiring rather than job losses, and is concentrated in roles built on codified, textbook-taught knowledge such as software engineering and customer service.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 4 asks how AI reshapes the route from qualification to livelihood. This is the clearest quantitative evidence yet that entry-level, knowledge-based graduate roles are narrowing first, sharpening the case for graduate capability work that goes beyond credentials.

Stanford Digital Economy Lab · University research institute report

entry.title: New Global South framework sets conditions for responsible generative AI in teaching
entry.summary:
A bibliometric and systematic review in the International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning traces the fast-growing literature on responsible generative AI in pedagogy and proposes a conceptual framework for the Global South. It finds research output led by the United States, China and Australia, while identifying ethical awareness, trust, institutional support, infrastructural readiness and AI competence as the conditions that most shape adoption.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 6 covers responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy. This framework gives Wits AHEAD a peer-reviewed reference point for judging when generative AI adoption in Southern universities is genuinely responsible rather than merely available.

International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: PISA 2025 finds 15-year-olds who skip AI chatbots for schoolwork outscore those who rely on them, as global reading skills fall sharply
entry.summary:
The OECD's PISA 2025 results, released on 8 September 2026, show reading scores falling by 28 points across OECD countries and by 16 points among other participating countries and economies between 2015 and 2025, one of the sharpest declines since the assessment began. The report finds that 15-year-olds who do not use AI chatbots for schoolwork generally score higher than those who do, and that more than one in four students say classmates are distracted by digital devices in most or every science lesson.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 5, analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, gains a stark systems-level signal here: a global assessment tying heavier reliance on AI chatbots to weaker outcomes, a caution Wits AHEAD weighs directly against its own pillar 1 work on generative AI in teaching and assessment.

OECD (PISA 2025 Results, Volume I) · Intergovernmental body report

entry.title: Indian researchers show synthetic student data can train dropout early-warning systems without exposing real records
entry.summary:
Researchers at Parul University in India, writing in the Nature journal Scientific Reports, built a machine-learning framework that trains dropout early-warning models on synthetic student data before fine-tuning with a small share of real records. Trained purely on 20,000 synthetic students across 180 courses, the model correctly identified 47.3 per cent of at-risk students by week four, and reached an accuracy score of 0.831 once fine-tuned with just a fifth of real data, close to the 0.842 benchmark set by training on real data alone.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 2, AI and predictive analytics for student success, gains a practical answer to a real constraint: universities that cannot share sensitive student records can still build reliable retention early-warning systems, a route Wits AHEAD can weigh for its own throughput and retention work.

Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: UNESCO-ICHEI dialogue in Kathmandu charts ethical, gender-inclusive AI integration for South Asian universities
entry.summary:
UNESCO's Kathmandu office, Tribhuvan University, the Asian Development Bank and UNESCO-ICHEI convened South Asian higher education leaders and government officials on 20 May 2026 to chart what a keynote by Shafika Isaacs called an inclusive and equitable AI ecosystem. The dialogue named uneven digital infrastructure, limited AI competencies among lecturers and fragmented national policies as the region's main barriers, launched an ICHEI Nepal National Centre at Tribhuvan University for AI capacity-building, and previewed a forthcoming report on digital transformation in South Asian higher education.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, and pillar 3, AI in STEM and teacher education, both feature directly: a regional capacity-building centre and a named commitment to full participation of girls and women in AI-related study and work offer a template Wits AHEAD can weigh against Southern Africa's own policy gaps.

UNESCO · UN agency article

entry.title: Cyprus study finds science teachers eager for AI but held back by confidence gaps and thin pedagogical training
entry.summary:
A Frontiers in Education study of 43 in-service STEM teachers in Cyprus, led by Christiana Karousiou and Maria Evagorou at the University of Nicosia, found that nearly 70 per cent rated technology as very important for learning outcomes, yet only 7 per cent felt confident using AI tools before training and 65.1 per cent lacked confidence with simulations and virtual tools. After training, teachers recognised AI's potential for personalised learning and automatic grading, but 83.7 per cent still cited a lack of pedagogical knowledge for using it well and 74.4 per cent worried it would weaken students' critical thinking.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar 3, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, is addressed squarely: the gap this study documents between teachers' enthusiasm and their readiness is exactly what Wits AHEAD's own teacher-education work aims to close.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: UNESCO report confronts AI's 'elephant in the room' questions for education
entry.summary:
UNESCO has published The Algorithm in the Room, a collection of 26 think pieces on how algorithmic systems are reshaping education, released to coincide with Digital Learning Week 2026 in Paris. The report organises contributions from students, educators, researchers and policymakers around six questions covering agency, relational development, pedagogy, cognition, governance and the future of education. It frames algorithmic systems as an urgent, largely unaddressed issue running through education systems worldwide.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the report offers Global South universities a structured set of governance questions to test their own AI policies against, rather than importing frameworks built for wealthier systems.

UNESCO · UN agency report

entry.title: South African universities move from detecting AI use to redesigning assessment
entry.summary:
North-West University, the University of Pretoria, Stellenbosch University and Wits are each rethinking how they handle generative AI, moving from detecting AI use towards redesigning assessment itself. Stellenbosch discontinued Turnitin's AI detector after finding it flagged 61.3 per cent of non-native English speakers' work as AI generated, against 5.1 per cent for native speakers, while North-West became the first South African university with a formal AI policy and has put more than 3,000 students through a free AI literacy course.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar one, generative AI in teaching, assessment and integrity, is being worked out in real time on South African campuses, with direct lessons for Wits AHEAD's own guidance on fair and reliable assessment.

TechCentral · Established South African technology press

entry.title: Study argues the EU AI Act requires rethinking STEM pedagogy, assessment and teacher agency
entry.summary:
A peer reviewed analysis by Konstantinos Kotsis and Georgios Stylos argues that the European Union's AI Act, combined with generative AI's growing capability, requires STEM educators to rebuild pedagogy, assessment and their own professional role together, rather than adopting AI tools piecemeal. The authors call for critical AI literacy that treats AI as an active participant in how knowledge is produced, process focused assessment that includes AI use declarations, and expanded teacher training in AI literacy and regulatory awareness.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Pillar three, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, gains a regulatory case study from Europe that Wits AHEAD can weigh against South Africa's own emerging AI policy framework.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: African Development Bank and La Francophonie launch digital skills and jobs partnership in five countries
entry.summary:
The African Development Bank and the International Organisation of La Francophonie have signed a partnership to expand digital skills training, entrepreneurship support and employment pathways for young people and women in Benin, Cameroon, Guinea, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar. The agreement, signed in Paris, covers training in web and mobile development, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and data analytics, building on the OIF's D-CLIC programme, which has already trained nearly 19,000 young people. A twelve to twenty four month pilot phase will run before any wider rollout to other member states.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This is a concrete test of pillar four, AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, in francophone Africa, and a model Wits AHEAD can point to when weighing AI skills partnerships elsewhere on the continent.

African Development Bank Group · Intergovernmental body press release

entry.title: Learning analytics study finds early-warning models plus relational feedback lift at-risk student engagement
entry.summary:
Researchers from Monash University, the University of Hong Kong and Vanderbilt University combined machine learning early warning models, which reached prediction accuracy above 0.8 AUC on new student cohorts, with relational feedback emails sent to students flagged as at risk. More than 30 per cent of flagged students went on to engage with previously unused learning activities within two weeks of receiving an intervention email, and most surveyed students wanted the emails sent more often than the twice a semester schedule tested.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar two, AI and predictive analytics for student success, the study shows prediction alone is not enough: pairing it with carefully designed, relational feedback is what moves engagement, a lesson directly relevant to Wits AHEAD's own early warning work.

Journal of Learning Analytics · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Universities UK roadmap calls for AI built into every degree, with the University of Surrey as its model
entry.summary:
Universities UK has published a Future Jobs Roadmap, drawn up with about 200 employers, business groups and universities, that asks every UK university to embed artificial intelligence within each degree programme rather than teach it as a separate digital skills module. The roadmap names the University of Surrey as an exemplar, where every course from foundation year to postgraduate level now carries a discipline specific AI component, overseen by an academic AI trailblazer, alongside a commitment to give all undergraduates access to meaningful work-based learning by 2035.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, it sets out a national model for weaving AI literacy into the discipline itself rather than bolting it on, a design question Wits AHEAD is also working through for curricula across the Global South.

University of Surrey · University announcement

entry.title: African Development Bank and Korea's KAIST sign three-year deal to build African AI and digital governance skills
entry.summary:
The African Development Bank and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology signed a three-year cooperation agreement in Seoul on 9 September, on the margins of the eighth Korea-Africa Economic Cooperation ministerial conference. The agreement covers joint research on AI related public policy and datasets, and training for African public officials, researchers and technical experts, and the Bank estimates AI could add up to a trillion dollars to Africa's economy by 2035.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 5, analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, it is a concrete channel for building the public sector research and policy capacity that African higher education and government systems need to use AI responsibly.

African Development Bank, reported by allAfrica · Intergovernmental body announcement

entry.title: Global survey of 45,000 students and staff finds AI use is high but guidance on using it well lags behind
entry.summary:
The Digital Education Council's AI in Higher Education Global Survey 2026, drawing on 45,398 responses from students and faculty across 35 countries, finds that 88 per cent of students and 77 per cent of faculty now use AI in their studies or teaching, up sharply on 2025. Only 29 per cent of students believe their lecturers are equipped to guide them on using AI well, and just 31 per cent of faculty feel meaningfully involved in shaping their institution's AI policy.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, the gap between fast adoption and slow guidance is exactly the governance and assessment integrity question Wits AHEAD tracks across its partner institutions.

Digital Education Council · Global survey report

entry.title: Ten-year review finds AI research in STEM education growing fortyfold since 2016, but concentrated in the Global North
entry.summary:
A bibliometric and qualitative review of 826 peer-reviewed studies published between 2016 and 2025, led by researchers at Ecuador's State University of Milagro, finds that annual publications on artificial intelligence in STEM education rose from four to 176 over the decade, with the United States and China producing the most output. The review identifies five dominant research themes, learning analytics, engineering education, AI literacy, immersive technology and generative AI, and flags a persistent geographical imbalance favouring the Global North, few long-term studies and weak ethical frameworks.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 3, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, the review confirms from the literature itself the gap Wits AHEAD exists to close, mapping where Global South research on AI in STEM teaching remains thin.

Frontiers in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article
